summary:
Indiana is a state within the United States, and a visitor to Indiana stands under the national framework on travel documents and entry. Indiana's own identity-document regime has tightened sharply. The Bureau of Motor Vehicles' ban on gender-marker changes to driver's licenses and state identification cards took effect on 1 February 2026, ending the long-standing route of obtaining such a change through a court order or physician statement. LGBTQ advocates who testified against the administrative rule change warned that it will forcibly out transgender and nonbinary residents whenever their documents are checked.

Birth certificates are closed as well. Transgender people could change the gender designation on an Indiana birth certificate by court order from 2014 until 2025, when Governor Mike Braun's March 2025 executive order defining sex solely as assigned sex at birth directed the Department of Health to stop updating markers. In May 2023 the Indiana Supreme Court had already declined, in split votes, to hear two cases seeking birth-certificate changes, leaving in place appeals-court rulings that trial courts lack authority to grant such changes unless the General Assembly codifies them. One of those cases involved a nine-year-old transgender girl whose male birth-certificate designation allowed her school to restrict her bathroom access. The state's X marker on identification was offered only between March 2019 and January 2020 before rejection following a March 2020 Attorney General opinion that only the General Assembly could authorize non-binary designations.

Facilities access is contested but, as of April 2026, Indiana law imposes no restriction on transgender people using restrooms aligned with their gender identity. Indianapolis and Bloomington ordinances expressly protect such use, and repeated criminal-ban proposals since 2021 have died in committee. An August 2023 Seventh Circuit decision upheld a preliminary injunction barring schools from limiting transgender students' bathroom use pending litigation. Senate Bill 182, which would designate multi-person restrooms, locker rooms and changing areas in public K-12 schools and state universities for use only by males or females based on reproductive biology at birth, passed the Indiana Senate on 27 January 2026 by a 37-8 party-line vote; it would also define sex and gender in statute, permanently bar birth-certificate amendments, restrict housing in prisons by birth sex, and restrict school and university sleeping facilities. The bill received no House hearing. Opponents including GenderNexus argued that its private right of action for anyone "directly or indirectly injured" would encourage harassment-style enforcement.

Gender-affirming care for minors is banned. Senate Bill 480, signed in April 2023 under an emergency clause, prohibits physicians from providing gender transition procedures to anyone under 18 or aiding such care, with a phase-out for existing patients; it was temporarily enjoined on 16 June 2023, took effect 27 February 2024 after a stay, and was upheld in November 2024 as a ban on surgery, puberty blockers and hormone therapy. House Bill 1569, signed April 2023 and effective 1 July 2023, bars use of state or federal funds for sexual reassignment surgery for incarcerated patients, exempting approvals granted before that date.

Indiana's hate-crimes law, enacted 3 April 2019, makes intent to harm or intimidate based on perceived or actual characteristics, including gender identity, an aggravating circumstance permitting enhanced sentences; before it, Indiana tracked bias crimes without sentencing enhancement. Employment protection for state workers on gender identity rests on 2004 and 2005 executive orders rather than statute, supplemented by county and city ordinances in Marion, Monroe, Tippecanoe and Vanderburgh counties. The April 2015 RFRA clarification bars denial of services, facilities, goods, employment, housing or public accommodation based on gender identity. Same-sex marriage has been recognized in Indiana since October 2014.

Erin In The Morning's February 2026 Anti-Trans National Legal Risk Assessment Map places Indiana among the harshest anti-trans states in the country, citing the 2026 identification policy and bathroom-ban escalation as drivers of adult risk.
tangentialFactors:
House Bill 1608, signed May 2023, prohibits classroom instruction on human sexuality in kindergarten through third grade and requires schools to notify a parent in writing if a non-emancipated minor requests use of a different name, pronoun or title. This creates an outing risk in school settings for gender-nonconforming minors and, by extension, for families visiting with children.

In May 2023 the governor signed a law barring city and county governments from enacting conversion-therapy bans by ordinance or executive order, leaving the practice legal statewide. This is a resident-facing harm but signals the legislative climate a visitor encounters.

Indiana's Religious Freedom Restoration Act of 26 March 2015 drew boycott threats and protests alleging targeting of LGBT rights; the 2 April 2015 clarification provides that it does not authorize refusal of services, facilities, goods, employment, housing or public accommodation based on sexual orientation or gender identity. The clarification's scope is a live question for anyone relying on it in a dispute.

The Seventh Circuit's April 2017 Hively v. Ivy Tech decision, binding in Illinois, Indiana and Wisconsin, holds that employment discrimination based on sexual orientation violates Title VII, though Indiana statutes still omit sexual orientation as a protected category. Federal statutory protection therefore does work that state statute does not.

Same-sex sexual activity was decriminalized in Indiana effective 1 July 1977. This is background to the current legal climate rather than a present-day risk.
